Video game consoles will bounce back – Here’s The Dring
Plus, the racing game Amazon abandoned has a new home
Christopher Dring
Aug 25, 2026
∙ Paid
Hello! Happy Monday. Are you heading to Gamescom? If so, maybe I’ll see you there. Although looking at my schedule, maybe not!
This week, we had the big GTA leak, and a couple of new studios opened. But the stories I’ve picked to dive into are around the worrying numbers around video game consoles.
Plus, a brand-new story (with some exclusive quotes) about Clutch, the Maverick Games racer that Amazon dropped earlier this year.
Enjoy!
‘Here’s The Dring’ is our subscriber-only edition of The Game Business. If you’d like to support us, we currently have a 75% off Summer Sale running. Not only do you receive this weekly newsletter and podcast, but we also produce a monthly market report and offer access to our events at no additional cost. Best of all? It also helps fund our main free Shows and newsletters on Tuesday and Thursday.
Consoles suffer their worst month of US sales in six years
In Brief: US console hardware revenue fell to a low not seen since July 2020, when PS4, Xbox One and Switch were in short supply due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Higher console prices, driven by the rising cost of RAM and storage, has ‘significantly’ impacted the selling rates of PS5 and Xbox Series S and X, says data firm Circana.
What You Need To Know:
July US sales of games, hardware and accessories fell 10% to $4.5 billion compared to the year before, reports Circana.
Mobile was the biggest reason for the decline, with console and PC content also dropping year-on-year.
Nintendo Switch 2 will receive a $50 price rise in September, potentially making the situation for console sales worst.
Data firm Ampere Analysis conducted a scenario analysis around what might happen if PlayStation 6 or Xbox’s Project Helix were to launch at $1,000. Assuming the new consoles are incrementally improved over the previous generation, the combined number of PS6 and Helix consoles sold after the first five years could be up to 38% lower than the combined sales of PS5 and Xbox Series S and X during the same period.
However, that isn’t a 38% total drop in console users, because there will be an increased number of players sticking with the previous generation.
Here’s The Dring:
The cinema has made quite the comeback (bear with me, this does relate to the topic).
2026 is set to be the biggest year for theatrical movies since before the pandemic. There are already five films that have exceeded $1 billion in Box Office revenue.
But… hadn’t we all decided that Netflix and the streaming wars had killed the big screen? What’s caused the resurgence?
The answer is incredibly boring… there were some popular films out. Inventive horror films, an ambitious sci-fi movie, a gothic romance and an adaptation of an epic poem. Interesting movies, ambitious movies, big franchise films and entirely new concepts. Stuff for kids, stuff for adults and everyone in-between.
It turns out for all the deep analysis of Gen Z viewing habits, the way to get people back to the cinema was to give people a reason to go back to the cinema.

Unity CEO: “The cost of building a game is coming down markedly”
CEO Matthew Bromberg gets optimistic about the future of video games
Christopher Dring
Aug 25, 2026
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Unity CEO Matthew Bromberg on…
Falling development costs
His positive outlook for the business
The AI ‘threat’
Plus, East vs West, the console sector, Epic Games and more
Last month, Unity CEO Matthew Bromberg took to the stage at the firm’s Unite conference in Seoul.
I watched his speech ahead of our interview, and I was struck by how positive it was. In the midst of studio closures, lay-offs, price rises and frustrated players, it was a refreshing listen.
“There is no question there’s been a tremendous amount of dislocation in our business and a lot of studios are retrenching,” Bromberg tells me. “It’s important to recognize that. We’re clearly in this moment of transition that is causing some pain.
“But I am absolutely 100% optimistic about the future. Having been doing this for some time, I’ve never spent a year in this business where people aren’t prone to doom and gloom. But the demand is not going anywhere. Human beings love interactive entertainment, and they love playing, and there is no evidence that there is some degradation in that desire.”
Matthew Bromberg at Unite Seoul
Beyond the simple fact that ‘people like games’, Bromberg is seeing a shift in how they’re being made.
“Although there’s all this disruption, the cost of building a game is coming down markedly. And that will continue. In my mind, there has never been a better time for independents to get together and make something extraordinary. I said that in Seoul. It used to be that the amount of resource you had to pour into something was the single biggest driver of whether or not you can be successful. Not that there weren’t lots of very high-profile flame outs, but the barrier was, ‘can I get 100, 200, 300 people together to do something? And can I pay for that for five years?’ That world is on the verge of changing radically.
“As a consequence, for those who are able to use the tools to take the power back in a way that creates opportunity for themselves and creates great art and entertainment for others, those folks are in a really great spot.”
Bromberg says that new platforms, like Netflix and Switch 2, are emerging. The platform economics on mobile are improving. And better games are on the way.
“The last few years was a period of optimization around known models and gameplay modalities, and that created a kind of sameness and sequelization, both literally and metaphorically,” he continues. “And it led to a disconnect between a lot of the major games that came out and how players received them. There was a lot of failure in that disconnect. But it’s hard to make hit games. It always has been and always will be. We will make great games, we’ll make them on new platforms, more people will make them than before, and everything will be fine.”
In today’s bumper edition of The Game Business Show , we chat to Bromberg about Unity’s turnaround, his approach to leadership, the AI ‘threat’, in-game ads, the future of consoles, Netflix, Unity’s friendship with Epic, the rise of China and Korea, and a whole lot more.
I’ve selected some of my favourite bits below. Alternatively, catch the entire chat via the links above.
Sponsor Message
Game-led creative production
Keywords Studios is the games industry’s end-to-end partner, with 13,000 people across 26 countries helping studios build, launch and support games at global scale. Supercharged by technology and shaped by long-term partnership, Keywords Studios connects specialist expertise around the player experience.
For global campaigns, that means creative production built around games and the audiences who play them. From trailers and key art to virtual production, campaign content and launch assets, Keywords Studios helps studios create content that understands the game, respects the audience and drives meaningful player connection.
The secret to turning around a business? Don’t be afraid
Three years ago, Unity was in trouble, not just from a business stand-point but also in the eyes of its clients who had lost trust in the firm following its controversial runtime fee plans (which it later cancelled).
Bromberg joined in 2024, and things have improved significantly since. In fact, it just delivered its best ever financial quarter.
The Unity CEO has been involved in these moments before. He helped turnaround Zynga, and at EA he rescued the MMO Star Wars: The Old Republic.
So, what’s his secret?
“It’s a really good environment to not be afraid in.”
“The most important thing is to be honest and fearless about what’s going wrong, what it is that people are unhappy about, and to authentically try to fix the problem,” he begins.
“No matter how difficult, no matter how painful, no matter how much change you have to make, no matter how much risk you need to take on, you have to commit to making it better.
“One issue that folks run into with these things is fear. They think, ‘Well, if I make all these changes, I might make it worse. The key to this whole thing is prioritization. We understand what people need and we’re going to deliver those things… but that means we’re not going to deliver a whole host of other things. And what if those things that I don’t deliver create a problem?’ Or, ‘if I’m going to make everything different, I’m probably going to have to change a lot of the people, and a lot of the ways we’re working, because it hasn’t produced the results. There’s going to be a tremendous amount of confrontation, awkwardness and pain in reformulating teams and changing executives.’
“You have to care more about the end result than you do about the daily pain. In my experience, usually folks know what the issues are to one degree or another, but they’re afraid to confront them because of what they imagine they’re going to have to do if that perception is correct. So, they pull back from understanding almost subconsciously.”
I observed there are probably a lot of companies that might benefit from that perspective.
“It’s a really good environment to not be afraid in,” he admits.
Western game developers can fight back with shorter dev cycles
Bromberg helped save The Old Republic at EA
At Unite Seoul, Bromberg highlighted the “extraordinary” rise in the number of hit games coming out of Korea and China. Certainly, the game business in those territories are in a better shape than in the US and parts of Europe.
But Bromberg is confident Western teams will battle back.
“Where the Western studios got into trouble is the development cycles, as they got elongated, that potential for dislocation with the player grows with each advancing day,” he tells us.
“When I first got to EA, I came in to run Star Wars: The Old Republic, which was an MMO that had gone very badly awry. It was a six-year development cycle, and in the six years lots of things changed, including subscription MMOs no longer being desired. It was free-to-play at that time. We had to reimagine everything fundamentally.
“What all game teams need to do is compress development cycles as much as possible, connect to players as early as possible, and build in conjunction with that player, and do that in an organic way so that when it releases, it feels connected to that community.
“The counterfactual which is, I go into a room for five years, I build this thing, and then ‘ta-da’. I made a cinematic and I expect a hit… that’s over. It’s just not going to happen anymore except for maybe a very tiny number of very highly anticipated titles. There needs to be a little bit of a rethink, and it’s happening.”
AI is not about to kill the video game industry
Earlier this year Google revealed Project Genie, which seemingly allowed people to make a video game with prompts. Multiple public game companies saw their share price fall sharply. Unity was one of those.
“Great games are still extraordinarily difficult to make,” Bromberg says. “This obsession around one-shotting games… if I had a dollar for every time I went on X, and somebody said, ‘I one-shotted this with 3DGS. The games business is over.’ People love to do that, and there’s nothing in the world I find more aggravating. And these are people who probably play lots of great games who know that it’s much more than that.”
“If I had a dollar for every time I went on X, and somebody said, ‘I one-shotted this with 3DGS. The games business is over.’ There’s nothing I find more aggravating.”
So, was he surprised how the markets reacted to Project Genie?
“It’s important to understand how the markets function now. It’s another artifact of how the world functions. Folks respond to memes. [I once told investors]: ‘My advice to you would be to not buy and sell shares based on LinkedIn posts.’ But of course, nobody cares what I think. They’re going to keep doing that. That’s the world we live in.
“And in fairness, creating a video game is a complex thing, and there aren’t a ton of people who understand what that process is like and what it requires, and how extraordinarily difficult it is. So, the fact that folks would react like that… at some level didn’t surprise me.
“But honestly, you don’t pay attention, up or down. When I started at the company, the first talk I gave I said: ‘You will have had the experience of doing the wrong thing and having the stock go up in the past. And you may have the experience now of doing the right thing and having it go down, and that’s fine. What you have to do is ground yourself in doing the right thing. And all the rest of it takes care of itself over time’.”
Console costs will go down and new games will bring in younger players
Unity works across all platforms, including PC, console, mobile… even Netflix and Fortnite. It knows where things are growing, and where things are challenged. And one area that appears challenged right now is the console space.
“It’s been a difficult time for console hardware, which is under genuine cost pressure,” Bromberg notes. “It’s unprecedented and it’s wacky. The idea that things get more expensive is the upside down of how it usually works. But that doesn’t mean that great console entertainment isn’t going to be consumed in massive quantities, and we’ll see that with GTA.
“I think of the cost pressures as being temporary. Clearly from a demographic perspective, the console is a little bit challenged as the core consumer ages. I’m not sure that the console business is replacing older players with as many younger players as it used to. But it was not very long ago that every teenager was playing Fortnite on console, so much so that it was thought to be a problem.
“The platform is vibrant. We will get more hit console entertainment. Costs will come down. And the industry will make games that will attract younger consumers over time.”
Indeed, it all comes down to the games, concludes Bromberg.
“There will be better, more engaging games built over the next ten years than were ever built over the prior ten. We’re just beginning to scratch the surface of the level of persuasion and the intensity of engagement that we’re going to achieve. It’s crazy to think that the best years of this business are not in front of us.”
Check out our full interview with Bromberg, which dives deeper into AI, discusses Unity’s ad business, its partnership with Epic, and more.
And then join us on Thursday for our Gamescom edition of The Game Business Show. Until then, thank you for reading.

And then join us on Thursday for our Gamescom edition of The Game Business Show. Until then, thank you for reading.

text:
